analysis.one_liner: Bans partisan gerrymandering and repeat redistricting, excludes undocumented immigrants from House apportionment, and imposes national voting rules including a photo ID mandate.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on January 22, 2026 and referred to three House committees, where it has sat with no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR MAP Act would do four things at once. It would require congressional maps to be compact and contiguous and forbid drawing districts to help a party or an incumbent, and it would let a state redraw its map only once per decade unless a court orders more. It would exclude undocumented immigrants from the population count used to apportion House seats and Electoral Votes. And it would overrule state choices on voting: states could not use ranked choice voting in federal elections, could not offer same-day registration, and would have to require photo ID for in-person voting and signature matching for mail ballots.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in states with aggressive gerrymandering would gain more competitive districts and fewer mid-decade remaps. If the map-drawing rules had real teeth, House elections would be less pre-decided. The photo ID and signature-match rules are framed as benefiting voters' confidence in election integrity, though their practical effect is debated.

how_it_helps.text: It requires congressional districts to be contiguous and as compact as practicable, and bars drawing them to favor or disfavor an incumbent, candidate, or party — directly attacking partisan gerrymandering.
It prohibits a state from redistricting more than once after each census unless a court orders it, which would stop mid-decade remaps aimed at flipping seats.
It requires photo ID for in-person voting and signature matching for mail ballots in federal elections, which its supporters describe as protecting ballot integrity.

analysis.who_pays: Undocumented immigrants and the states where they live, which would lose House seats and Electoral Votes under the new apportionment count. Voters without a qualifying government-issued photo ID, and voters in states that currently use same-day registration or ranked choice voting in federal elections, would face new barriers. Parties that benefit from drawing maps to their advantage would lose that tool.

drawbacks.text: Excluding undocumented immigrants from the apportionment count would shift House seats and Electoral Votes away from states with larger immigrant populations, changing how the House reflects the actual population.
It would overrule states that have adopted ranked choice voting for federal elections, removing an option several states have chosen for themselves.

The national photo ID and signature-match requirements and the ban on same-day registration take away tools states currently use to make voting easier, and voters who lack qualifying ID or who register late could find it harder to cast a ballot.

The anti-gerrymandering rules say districts should not favor a party or incumbent, but they give no enforcement mechanism beyond federal court challenges, and the bill requires those challenges to be brought in federal district court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The good-faith case for the bill is real: a ban on drawing districts to favor a party or incumbent, a compactness requirement, and a one-map-per-decade rule would take some of the gaming out of House elections. But the bill bundles that reform with three provisions that cut the other way: it shrinks the population base used to allocate House seats and Electoral Votes, blocks states from using ranked choice voting, and overrides state laws in order to require photo ID and end same-day registration. The voting and apportionment changes are the larger part of the bill, and their costs — reduced representation for states with large immigrant populations and more ballot access requirements — fall mainly on specific groups of ordinary people. The anti-gerrymandering rules are worth having; the package is badly designed to get them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and referred to three committees, and no committee has taken it up since, so nothing has happened to it yet.

narrative.text: Representative Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced the FAIR MAP Act on January 22, 2026.

The bill was referred to three committees at once — Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration — a referral pattern that spreads jurisdiction thin and often means no single committee takes the lead.
It has one cosponsor, a Republican, and no further action has been recorded since introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — the bill has simply gone nowhere in committee. If it stays there, the winners are the map-drawers and state officials whose current practices it would restrict.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Michael Lawler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three committees

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor; no votes have been taken, so the partisan shape of support or opposition is not yet known.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state parties that benefit from gerrymandered maps
industries.note: The bill bars districts drawn to favor a party or incumbent and allows only one redistricting per decade, reducing parties' and incumbents' ability to engineer safe seats. This is the provision that most directly serves ordinary voters.

industries.industry: State legislatures and map-drawers in states with large immigrant populations
industries.note: Excluding undocumented residents from the apportionment count would shift House seats and Electoral Votes toward whiter, lower-immigration states and away from states with large immigrant communities.

industries.industry: Major-party ballot administrators and two-party election structures
industries.note: Banning ranked choice voting removes a method some states use to allow more candidates to compete without spoilers, preserving the two-candidate status quo in federal elections.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with no cosponsors beyond one and no committee action. Election-procedure bills referred simultaneously to three committees rarely advance, and this one has no signs of a markup. Most likely it stays in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress.
